steps.read: A note on how the manuscript was made: voice memos, journalist agent, librarian, review board, and a pre-publication candidate that is explicitly not a version. I also scanned the contents: 41 chapters in 10 parts, 75,000 words, and some chapters admitted to be placeholders.
steps.thought: Honest, but this is a production diary, not a cover letter. A commissioning editor wants to know what the book is and who buys it, and this front matter spends its words on process. Placeholders in a manuscript I am asked to price worry me.
steps.quote: Where the sources run out, the chapter says so, in a note addressed to Dinis.
steps.question: Is this a second edition or a new book? The note says it is still undecided.
steps.confusion: The cast of roles (board, advocate, cutter, checker) is explained to someone who has not yet been told what the book is about.
steps.next: Read on: the proposal is chapter 1, so I read it properly.

steps.read: The pitch. Two readers, Gen Z entering work and Gen X subject-matter experts, joined as Gen ZX with a ZX Spectrum hook. The stated objective is that the reader starts a GenAI company by the end. The measure of success is companies created.
steps.thought: This is a real hook and a clear audience: the expert founder aged 40 to 55 is a buyer I recognise. The objective is bold, and bold objectives can be failed in public. The 'XZ backdoor' aside and the Spectrum nostalgia are charming but the book then promises company-formation content I suspect is not there.
steps.quote: Our job is to empower the reader to create a startup by the end of the book.
steps.question: Who verifies the 'fastest-growing one in a thousand' founder statistic, and is it a figure I could put on a cover?
steps.confusion: The same chapter says it is for two generations and then says millennials can read it too; the buyer is blurred.
steps.next: The proposal has a hook. Check the contents and the first part.

steps.read: A two-line part introduction listing five chapters.
steps.thought: Nothing to judge. Five chapters before the argument starts is a lot of runway for a business reader.
steps.next: Read chapter 2 for the opening voice.

steps.read: Wonder and optimism: 'you are lucky to be here', the list of technology waves the author lived through, the dot-com crash, and a rebuttal of AI fear. The author admits he could not read the Business Insider piece and cannot name the podcaster.
steps.thought: Warm, personal, a real voice. But several unsourced anecdotes and an admission of not having read the article he rebuts weaken it for a sceptical trade reader. A book that opens with 'lucky to be here' sells on mood, and mood dates fast.
steps.quote: I could not get past the paywall, so I cannot tell you what it argued.
steps.question: Why does a published book's opening rebut an article the author could not read?
steps.confusion: Notes to Dinis inside the chapter body make it hard to tell what is the book and what is the working draft.
steps.next: Skim the graphs chapter, then jump to the technical frame.

steps.read: Graphs as networks of nodes and edges, the detective board, Wardley maps as graphs with positions, code as a layered graph. A claim about an sgit commit reaching nine of 72 commands.
steps.thought: Interesting if you already like graphs. For a business-book buyer it is a big conceptual ask this early, and it leans on the author's own tool as the proof.
steps.quote: What is crazy is to make decisions based on shadows of reality.
steps.question: Why does a founder need a chapter on code as a fractal graph before they have formed a company?
steps.confusion: Jumps from the detective board to AST and call trees without warning.
steps.next: Skip ahead to the frame, then sample what each part promises.

steps.read: What generative AI is, in the author's working picture, followed by a list of corrections an AI agent made to him (vectors not graphs, the prompt does not change the model, hallucination has a second cause). The title note explains the Gen ZX name.
steps.thought: The corrections section is unusual and honest, but it also tells me the main explanation is a metaphor the author knows is wrong. For a non-technical reader the 'working picture' is clear; the corrections are for experts. The Lee Brimelow image is a rights problem I would have to clear.
steps.quote: I asked the agent that is helping me write this book to correct me where I was wrong.
steps.question: Which of these two pictures is the one the book relies on later, the metaphor or the correction?
steps.confusion: The chapter teaches a picture and then undoes it in the same chapter.
steps.next: Jump to the first part about jobs, then the centre of the book.

steps.read: Hired for the workflow. Operator skills, hiring statistics from several surveys, the advice to send a tailored analysis with your CV.
steps.thought: Practical and sellable to the Gen Z half, packed with statistics from LinkedIn, Microsoft, PwC and Gartner, which will date within a year. Useful for a trade promotion if sourced to the letter.
steps.quote: An edge is not a job.
steps.question: Who checks 1,165 percent and 62 percent against the originals before print?

steps.read: Sessions, briefs, role files, shared state, and rules that grow. Counts of commits and messages from the author's own repositories.
steps.thought: The substance is real and the 'every mistake added a rule' line is a good one. But the evidence is the author's own newsroom; to my reader it is a case study of one company.
steps.quote: Every mistake added a rule, and every new rule caused new mistakes.
steps.question: Which of this is advice for my reader's first company and which is the newsroom's internal practice?
steps.confusion: Sessions named with an @ prefix and the Librarian are introduced as if known.
steps.next: Now the centre of the book, Start the company.

steps.read: Part introduction for the centre of the edition: ship, price, sell, fund, make the company real. Flagged as not legal or tax advice.
steps.thought: This is the part the whole objective stands on. Six chapters; I will sample two.
steps.quote: From experience, mine and the people I work with; not legal or tax advice.
steps.next: Read the pricing chapter, then the company chapter.

steps.read: Four moves to a product: define, price, deliver at linear cost, offer free to people who know you. Free is not zero. Pay-after-value, the Stripe fee arithmetic, a reading meter at 10p an article.
steps.thought: Best chapter so far. Concrete numbers, a counter-example, an honest 'no results yet'. It is built on the author's own RiskMandate ladder, which makes it read as a case study of his company. The meter is a live experiment on his site, which I cannot sell as evidence.
steps.quote: A commercial product is one people take when the only cost is their own attention.
steps.question: What happens to the argument if the reading-meter review on 6 December 2026 fails?
steps.next: Read the company chapter, the one the objective depends on.

steps.read: A chapter that says it is a placeholder. Two lines on Portugal and Lithuania, a section on Upwork, two notes to Dinis asking for memos.
steps.thought: This is the book's central promise and it is empty. The UK company formation, EU programmes and cloud credits are what a founder buys the book for. A publisher cannot take a manuscript where the headline objective is a stub.
steps.quote: This chapter is a placeholder, and it says so.
steps.question: When will the memos exist, and will the book wait for them?
steps.confusion: The title lists four jurisdictions and the text delivers essentially none.
steps.next: Check the sgit and privacy chapters, since the author's own products come in there.

steps.read: Encrypted version control, the vault key, read keys, write-only lanes, key management, two corrections (constraints, GDPR). Quotes from the EDPB, ICO and the Court of Justice.
steps.thought: Well argued and carefully hedged, including 'None of this is legal advice'. But it is the author's product, beta, with a brief essay in the middle on why nobody buys it for the encryption. As a publisher I see a product chapter inside a business book, which has costs for trust and for shelf life.
steps.quote: that last part is a feature with a real cost, which I would rather say up front than have you find out
steps.question: Is a reader supposed to adopt sgit, or just understand the principle?
steps.confusion: Dense terms (append token, read key, vault of vaults) arrive faster than they are defined.
steps.next: Check the hands-on part, which should be what readers act on.

steps.read: A folder per contact, five documents each, a six-line agent policy, a one-week exercise plan. Clear and usable.
steps.thought: The most usable chapter, and the kind of thing I can put on a back cover. The contents list a 'Your first workspace' chapter in Part 4 that looks like the same idea, so I suspect it is duplicated across Part 4 and Part 9.
steps.quote: Draft and never send; append and never rewrite; stay in the folder.
steps.question: Why is this workflow in the book twice?
steps.next: Check the form-your-company chapter, then the ending.

steps.read: Another placeholder: what the chapter will cover, three facts, five decisions to make before registering.
steps.thought: Second stub for the same missing content. The five decisions are sensible but they are a checklist where a procedure was promised.
steps.quote: By the end of this chapter you will have a company: registered, with a name, a country and a bank account.
steps.question: How can a chapter promise a registered company when it says the steps are not written?
steps.next: Read the last chapter, then decide.

steps.read: How the book was made: repository and vault, roles, articles as briefs, the review board, release candidates. Then the credit to Claude, the voice inputs, the ratio of words, and a request to email the author about companies started.
steps.thought: I have seen enough. The AI co-writing is disclosed clearly but at the very end, and the book describes itself as a process product as much as a book. The measure of success is a single email address belonging to the author's other product. The pitch is strong, the delivery has holes, and the ending is a methodology essay, not a send-off.
steps.quote: This book is co-written with Claude, and I want to say so and credit it.
steps.question: How would a reader act on this chapter if they want a book, not a newsroom?
steps.confusion: The chapter and the 'About' note both explain the process, so the explanation appears twice.
steps.next: Stop and decide. I have read the proposal, a chapter from the middle parts and the end.

steps.read: Two-line intro to the frame part.
steps.thought: Fine, nothing to say.

steps.read: Wardley maps introduced by drawing one first, the four stages, where do you fit, centre of gravity, jobs that never scaled.
steps.thought: Good teaching device, drawing before naming. But it is a third conceptual framework (graphs, maps, lenses) before any company is formed.
steps.quote: A map you cannot be wrong about is a diagram.
steps.question: Does a first-time founder need Wardley maps to follow the later chapters?
steps.confusion: The 'how to use this book' section tells readers to jump by centre of gravity, which conflicts with the instruction in chapter 2 not to skip.

steps.read: Steve Jobs dots, SG/Send as the author's own dot, multidisciplinary edge, maths teaching, learning, thinking with the AI.
steps.thought: Motivational, a generic trade-business chapter with some personal evidence. Could be shortened.
steps.quote: Your job now is to make dots worth connecting.
steps.confusion: Sections on maths teaching drift away from the founder theme.

steps.read: Lenses, roles, loops, tools, memory, and why long chats are compressed.
steps.thought: A good plain-language explanation of agents, which my reader needs. Chapter 32 then repeats the five-lens example, and chapter 33 repeats the loop.
steps.quote: Each of those roles is, in essence, almost a raw model plus a role description and a question.

steps.read: Anyone who can brief an agent is a developer; spreadsheets, errors, Portuguese as a programming language, what a briefing-only developer cannot do.
steps.thought: Good for the Gen X expert. The spreadsheet error statistics are a strong hook for a book cover.
steps.quote: Of 54 spreadsheets audited between 1997 and 2000, no fewer than 49 were found to contain significant errors
steps.question: The section on what the briefing-only developer cannot do is thin and flagged as such. Can it be answered?

steps.read: Explorer coding versus vibe coding, handover, villagers, bonus tests, no new features while you move.
steps.thought: The renaming is a good hook and probably the book's most shareable idea. The handover material has substance.
steps.quote: What people call vibe coding is exploration, and the word should say so.
steps.question: Does anyone outside the author's circle use 'explorer' and 'villager'?
steps.confusion: Wardley's explorer, villager and town planner terms are used without a quick refresher.

steps.read: Intro to getting the job, or making it.
steps.thought: Good framing of the old chapter becoming a new one.

steps.read: Act as the job you want, the 2018 echo, do it in public, put your CV online.
steps.thought: Solid, easy to market to the Gen Z half. Quoted back to the 2018 book heavily.
steps.quote: the bottom line is the same: if you are looking for a job, you have time

steps.read: Publish constantly, the author's unfinished books on Leanpub, a book as a curated set of finished articles.
steps.thought: Disarming that the author lists his stalled books, but a publisher reading that note takes it seriously: who finishes this one?
steps.quote: a book is a curated, ordered set of finished articles, plus the editorial thread that connects them.
steps.question: What guarantees this book is finished, given the stalled ones?

steps.read: The row becomes a folder: Record, Ledger, Messages, Notes, Summary, a six-line agent policy, five exercises.
steps.thought: This is the same workflow as chapter 30. Cut one or merge.
steps.quote: No developer, no new tool, no code.
steps.question: Which of the two is the canonical version?
steps.next: Skim part 4 and move to part 5.

steps.read: Intro to working with agents.
steps.thought: Part 4 is only two chapters, one of them overlapping with chapter 30.

steps.read: Intro to direction and judgement.
steps.thought: Two chapters; good topic for a business book.

steps.read: Direction is the scarce skill, places of highest leverage, knowing when to stop, a budget per step, agents decide and people answer.
steps.thought: One of the strongest ideas in the book and well suited to the executive market.
steps.quote: Direction is the scarce thing.

steps.read: Ask for evidence, provenance, how to disagree rationally, reality corrects the graph, be the best-prepared person.
steps.thought: Useful but long and returns to graphs; chapter 35 repeats the preparation point.
steps.quote: Karl Popper's principle is short: a claim earns its status by being refutable.
steps.confusion: The 'privacy and Snapchat' passage is a side trip.

steps.read: The playbook that worked, why experts were always the better bet, where the opening is, where the company sits, there is a company in this.
steps.thought: The most direct statement of the audience. Discloses that two of the three expert founders are people the author helps; I would want that disclosed more loudly.
steps.question: Are the three expert founders real, named and willing to be quoted?

steps.read: Ship it, give it away then take it away, five days and ten customers, the loop is the moat.
steps.thought: Good argument and a good story, though the story is about the author's own product.
steps.quote: Not to plan, not to pitch, not to architect. Ship.
steps.question: Is the ten-customers story typical or exceptional?
steps.confusion: The text notes its own tension with 'vibe coded' versus explorer coding.

steps.read: Sell: answer the question in the room, sell value that lands the day they switch, sell a service before the product, what the buyer is about to do to you.
steps.thought: Credible and specific. Mentions a named consultant, which needs permission.
steps.quote: impressed by evidence and bored by claims

steps.read: Do not raise before you are profitable; who investors choose; sell rather than issue shares; what breaks.
steps.thought: A contrarian view with a flagged bias (the author's companies run on open source). Needs a legal read before print.
steps.quote: The worst possible time to raise money is before you are profitable, before you have the product, before you understand the fit.

steps.read: Intro to building without a server.
steps.thought: Part 7 is where the author's products cluster.

steps.read: Serverless defined by what it costs when idle, with a pricing table dated 18 October 2026, cloud as Lego, files as the database.
steps.thought: The by-the-hour test is a good practical rule. The table will be out of date within a year.
steps.quote: Ship your company serverless.
steps.question: Will the table be refreshed for each printing?

steps.read: Mandate, reach and the gap for agents, the policy beside the prompt, who can pull the plug, secrets.
steps.thought: Good for corporate bulk buyers. It is also the pitch for RiskMandate.
steps.quote: A control bounds a grant only if it is enforced by something the grant does not include.
steps.question: Where does the advice end and the product begin?

steps.read: Open source: what it is and is not, the fork next door, not free, all of it or an evaluation version, sell the build not the code.
steps.thought: Useful and fair, but it reinforces the free-edition risk: the author's argument is that giving it away is the strategy.
steps.quote: It was never about contributions.
steps.question: Does the author's open-source stance cover this book's CC BY licence in the way that hurts print sales?

steps.read: A release that passed every check and never reached anybody; green does not mean live; tests, twins, and five synthetic people.
steps.thought: A strong story, but engineering-heavy for a founder reader.
steps.quote: Getting a working thing into a stranger's hands is still, in 2026, genuinely hard
steps.confusion: The 'five people who do not exist' section is unexplained at skim level.

steps.read: Intro to the long game: graphs as memory and civic responsibility.
steps.thought: A short part at the back of the book that feels like an epilogue, but a heavy one.

steps.read: Backup your life, thinking in graphs, memory as context management, publish and the site becomes the memory.
steps.thought: Third graph chapter; this is the book's personal philosophy and risks going on.
steps.quote: You basically need to backup your life!

steps.read: Portugal, the OWASP keynote, EU regulation, state-paid code belongs to the commons, smaller models, sovereignty.
steps.thought: Interesting, and interesting for the Portugal and EU market, but it is a policy chapter in a startup book. A Portuguese edition may be the real home for it.
steps.quote: It only takes courage, focus and commitment
steps.question: Is this chapter for founders or for policymakers?

steps.read: Intro to the eleven hands-on workflows, dated 2026.
steps.thought: Good idea to date and renew them each year, which suits a series of annual editions.

steps.read: Draw a graph of something you know, a question not a subject, forty-odd lines in a text file.
steps.thought: Practical and the failure mode (picking a subject) is spot on.
steps.quote: if somebody tells you otherwise in the first month, they are solving a different problem from yours

steps.read: Five-lens exercise on an idea of your own.
steps.thought: Repeats the five-lens passage from chapter 7 almost word for word. Merge.
steps.confusion: I could not tell what this adds to chapter 7.

steps.read: Run an agent loop by hand with yourself as the harness.
steps.thought: Again restates chapter 7, but with an exercise. Good teaching if the earlier version is trimmed.
steps.quote: That is where the control lives.

steps.read: Storyboards as data drawn in the browser, checked quotes, the cast.
steps.thought: This is about how the website works. It reads as documentation for the author's own site, not a reader skill.
steps.quote: There is no image file to edit.
steps.question: Who is the reader for this recipe?
steps.confusion: I do not understand why a founder would build storyboards.

steps.read: Meeting briefs and follow-ups, a short chapter with the author's step by step still missing.
steps.thought: Useful idea, unfinished.
steps.quote: Now it is a brief and a feedback loop.

steps.read: Eight steps for a newsroom site and an inbox agent.
steps.thought: Another recipe tied to the author's site. Fine as an appendix.

steps.read: A table of startup credits and programmes as of 7 October 2026.
steps.thought: Commercially valuable to a founder, shelf life of months, and the unnamed vendors will be obsolete before the ink dries. Better as a web page.
steps.quote: Programmes change; check before applying.
steps.question: Who updates it, and when?

steps.read: Price it first, offer to people who know you, write a stop rule, count.
steps.thought: Repeats chapter 19's four moves, now as a workflow.
steps.confusion: The four moves appear in nearly identical words in chapter 19.

steps.read: A weekend recipe: static site, vault data, a model on the page, a payment link.
steps.thought: The most satisfying promise in the book, and it leans on the author's vault tool.
steps.quote: If it bills you by the hour when nobody is using it, it is not serverless.
steps.question: Can this be done without the sgit vault for readers who do not adopt it?

steps.read: Intro to the last part: how the book was made and the measure.
steps.thought: The process is the product, says the author; I disagree for a trade book.

put_down.why: I have read the proposal, sampled one chapter from the opening, middle, hands-on and final parts, and found the two chapters that carry the book's central promise are stubs. I know enough to decide.

buy_at_put_down.format: paperback if the company chapters are written; otherwise I would not publish
buy_at_put_down.would_pay: £19.99 paperback, £9.99 ebook, only for the finished version
buy_at_put_down.why: The hook and audience are real, but the central chapters are placeholders, the first edition is free, and the author's products take up a lot of space. I would sign only against a written plan for the missing chapters.

interview: A practical, personal argument that people with expertise in a field, and the generation entering work, can now build and start a GenAI company themselves, with agents, without servers, written in the first person by a security and software practitioner.

It is for the founder in their forties or fifties with twenty years in a problem, and for the Gen Z reader entering work. The Gen X half is for me: chapters 1, 8, 9, 15, 17 to 21 are the ones I could sell. The Gen Z job-hunting chapters 10 to 12 sit awkwardly next to a founder book.

Mostly, yes, in the argument and the numbers that are shown with their sources (chapters 14 and 19 especially). I believed it less where it relies on the author's own products as proof (chapters 24, 25, 39) and where it cannot read its own source (chapter 2's paywall). The honest hedging made me trust the author, and the 'For Dinis' notes made me trust the process while worrying about the text.

Chapter 3, on code as a fractal graph, lost me because I could not see why a founder needs it. Chapter 6 made me guess which picture the book relies on. Chapters 22 and 37 lost me by delivering nothing on the title.
It drags in chapters 2, 3 and 5 (opening and philosophy), and in Part 9 where chapters 32, 33 and 39 repeat earlier material. It rushes chapters 22, 35 and 37, which are stubs or one-page promises.

The order of the parts is sound until the end: frame, jobs, agents, judgement, company, serverless, long game, hands-on, process. I would merge chapters 13 and 30, merge 32 into 7, cut or move chapter 34 and 36 to a companion web page, move the process chapter 41 into an appendix, and bring Start the company forward to follow chapter 9 so the objective arrives sooner.

Chapter 15 on direction, chapter 19 on pricing with the Stripe arithmetic, chapter 9's renaming of vibe coding as explorer coding, and chapter 14's 'every mistake added a rule'. I would send chapter 19 to a founder I know.
Chapters 22 and 37, the placeholders, followed by chapter 41's process explanation and the repeated recipes. Also the notes to Dinis sitting in the text.

Both. The voice is clearly a person's: stories, opinions, mistakes. But the build method is machine-shaped: 'By the end of this chapter you will have' repeated in Part 9, uniform chapter lengths around 2,200 words, and statistics piled up in a pattern. The author says so himself in chapter 41, which is the right thing, but late.

Not as it stands. I would pay £9.99 for the ebook and £19.99 for the paperback once the company chapters exist. If the first edition is free and this one is free to read online too, the paperback is a gift or a reference, and I would price it at £16.99 to £19.99.
Write the company chapters. The promise of the book is that by the end you have started a company, and the UK, Lithuania, Portugal and EU chapters do not exist.
Yes: to a founder who has twenty years in a regulated field and has said 'I wish someone would build this'. Not to a Gen Z reader first; for them the job chapters feel like a different book.
Yes with conditions: the missing company chapters written, a clear single audience, and a cut of 20 to 25 percent of repeated and process material.

Business and technology shelf, founders and startups, next to books about AI for entrepreneurs. Online it sells under AI for founders, and as a gift to a family member who has an idea. Corporate bulk orders would suit the agent-control chapters.

Market: a crowded AI shelf where two of my own did differently. Dating: the programme tables, price and statistics. Free first edition and a free online edition. The author's own products (sgit, SG/Send, RiskMandate) throughout. Advice that reads as legal or tax advice in chapters 21 and 24, despite the disclaimers. The AI co-writing, which some bookshops will notice. And the 'second edition or new book' question remains undecided.

Title: I would drop 'Generation Z Developers' from the front and sell 'Gen ZX' or a plain 'Start a GenAI Company'. Length: cut towards 60,000 words by merging the duplicated chapters. Audience: lead with the expert founder. Structure: move the process to an appendix and bring the company part forward.

A platform: a mailing list, a talk circuit, a named set of founders who used it. Endorsements from two or three founders and an investor who has read it. A date: a finished manuscript with the company chapters written, and a plan for refreshing the programme tables each year.
rating_why: A strong hook, a clear audience and a few excellent chapters, held back by empty company chapters, repeated material and heavy use of the author's own products.

decision.why: I would commission it only after the UK, Lithuania, Portugal and EU chapters exist, the duplicated chapters are merged, the process is moved to an appendix, and the free first edition and online edition are addressed in the contract. The hook and the expert founder audience are worth it.

findings.what: The book's stated objective is that the reader has started a company by the end, but the chapters that say how (the company itself, and Form your company) are placeholders that only list what is missing. A publisher cannot sign a book whose headline promise is a stub.
findings.quote: This chapter is a placeholder, and it says so.

findings.what: Chapter 37 opens by promising a registered company with a bank account, then says the steps are not written. A reader who bought for this would feel misled.
findings.quote: By the end of this chapter you will have a company: registered, with a name, a country and a bank account.

findings.what: The Contacts folder, five documents and six-line agent policy appear in chapter 13 and again in chapter 30, and the five-lens example in chapter 7 recurs in chapter 32 and the four pricing moves in chapter 19 recur in chapter 39. Repetition pads the length and tires the reader.
findings.quote: Draft and never send; append and never rewrite; stay in the folder.

findings.what: Large parts of the middle and end are the author's own products (sgit, SG/Send, RiskMandate), used as the evidence for the argument. It is disclosed, but the book reads at times as a product tour, and the free-to-read online edition makes it look more like marketing.
findings.quote: that last part is a feature with a real cost, which I would rather say up front than have you find out

findings.what: The co-writing with Claude and the method are disclosed in the last chapter, after 40 chapters in the first-person voice. The disclosure is honest but late, and the About note and chapter 41 explain the process twice.
findings.quote: This book is co-written with Claude, and I want to say so and credit it.

findings.what: Notes addressed to Dinis are embedded throughout the chapters and several chapters admit to unnamed sources or unread articles, which shows how the draft was made but would have to be resolved before print.
findings.quote: I could not get past the paywall, so I cannot tell you what it argued.

findings.what: Dated tables of programmes, credits and prices (chapters 23 and 38) and many statistics (chapter 10) have a shelf life of months. They belong on a web page or in an annual update, not in the printed text.
Chapter 34 on storyboards drawn by code documents the author's own site and does not help a reader start a company.
findings.quote: There is no image file to edit.

recommendations: Write the company chapters (the UK limited company, Lithuania, Portugal, EU programmes, the first customers) before any contract is signed, and bring Start the company forward so the objective is delivered earlier.
Merge the duplicated chapters: 13 with 30, 32 into 7, 39 into 19, and cut chapters 34 and 36 to a web companion.
Move chapter 41 and the About note into one short appendix on how the book was made, and put the Claude co-writing disclosure on the cover or in the opening pages.
Pick one lead audience, the expert founder, and keep the Gen Z job chapters shorter or place them in a companion section.
Reduce the weight of the author's own products: give each a short case study and show at least one example that does not use sgit or RiskMandate.
Move dated tables (programmes, credits, prices) and time-sensitive statistics to a web page refreshed each year, and have every figure checked against its original before print.
Resolve all the notes to Dinis, clear the Lee Brimelow image rights, get permission for named people, and get a legal read of the funding, GDPR and tax passages.
Settle the title and edition question, and agree in the contract how the free online edition and the free first edition relate to the paid book.
